entry.title: Speculative Decoding: Faster Language Model Inference Without Changing the Output

link.title: Speculative Decoding: Faster Language Model Inference Without Changing the Output

entry.content:
A large language model writes text one token at a time. Each token needs a full pass through the network, and the next token cannot start until the previous one is known. This is the main reason that generating a long answer feels slow even on expensive hardware, and it is the reason that a lot of current research is about making each of those steps cheaper or fewer.

Speculative decoding takes a different route. It does not shrink the model, change its weights, or approximate its output. A small, fast model guesses several tokens ahead, and the large model checks all the guesses at once. Tokens that pass the check are kept. The procedure can be designed so that the final text has exactly the same distribution as if the large model had generated it alone. The idea was introduced independently by Leviathan, Kalman, and Matias [1] and by Chen et al. [2].

This post explains why it works, proves the correctness claim, derives how much speedup to expect, and tests both claims with a short NumPy program. If you have not seen how a language model produces tokens, the post on how LLMs work covers the background. You only need basic probability here.

Why decoding is slow

Generating a token with a model of \(P\) parameters takes about \(2P\) floating-point operations, one multiply and one add per weight. That is not much work for a modern accelerator. The trouble is that every one of those weights has to be read from memory to do it. For a 7-billion-parameter model stored in 16-bit precision, that is about 13.5 GB of data moved per token. A GPU with roughly 2 TB/s of memory bandwidth needs at least 6.7 ms just to stream the weights once, however fast its arithmetic units are, which caps generation near 150 tokens per second for a single sequence. The arithmetic intensity, the number of operations per byte moved, is about 1 for this workload, while the hardware can sustain on the order of 150. The chip spends most of its time waiting for memory [3].

That observation points to the opportunity. If the model is waiting on memory rather than on arithmetic, then asking it to process several tokens in a single pass costs very little extra. The weights are read once either way. The only question is where to find several tokens worth processing when we do not yet know what the next one is.

Checking is cheaper than writing

A transformer with a causal mask computes, in one forward pass, the next-token distribution at every position of the input. When we train the model, we use exactly this property: feed in a whole sentence, and get a prediction for each token from the tokens before it. At generation time we normally waste it, because we only have one new position to look at.

Suppose that someone hands us a candidate continuation of \(\gamma\) tokens. We can feed the context plus the candidate into the large model in a single pass and obtain its distributions at all \(\gamma + 1\) relevant positions. In the memory-bound regime described above, that costs roughly as much as generating one token, because the weights are read from memory only once either way. The candidate can come from several places. A smaller model that shares the large model’s vocabulary is the standard source, and it is the one we use here. (Proposers without a probability model, such as lookup of repeated n-grams, can be handled by treating their proposal as a distribution with all its mass on one token.) The remaining problem is to decide which of the proposed tokens to keep, in a way that does not distort the output.

The algorithm

Call the large model the target and the small one the draft. Let \(p(\cdot)\) be the target’s next-token distribution and \(q(\cdot)\) the draft’s, at whatever position we are discussing. One round of speculative decoding does the following.

  1. Draft. The draft model samples \(\gamma\) tokens autoregressively, \(x_1, \dots, x_\gamma\), recording its distribution \(q_i\) at each step.
  2. Score. The target model runs once on the context plus the draft tokens and returns its distributions \(p_1, \dots, p_{\gamma+1}\). Here \(p_i\) is the target’s distribution for position \(i\) given the context and the first \(i-1\) draft tokens.
  3. Verify. Go through the draft tokens from left to right. Accept \(x_i\) with probability \(\min\!\big(1,\; p_i(x_i)/q_i(x_i)\big)\).
  4. Repair. At the first rejection, discard that token and everything after it. Sample a replacement from the residual distribution \(p'_i\), defined just below, and end the round.
  5. Bonus. If all \(\gamma\) draft tokens are accepted, sample one more token from \(p_{\gamma+1}\). This is free, since the target already computed that distribution.

The residual distribution keeps only the probability mass by which the target exceeds the draft, and rescales it to sum to one:

\[p'_i(x) = \frac{\max\big(0,\; p_i(x) - q_i(x)\big)}{\sum_{y} \max\big(0,\; p_i(y) - q_i(y)\big)}.\]

Every round therefore emits between 1 and \(\gamma + 1\) tokens and costs one target pass plus \(\gamma\) draft passes. In the worst case we get one token per round, which is what ordinary decoding would have given us, plus the wasted cost of the draft.

A small example makes the rule concrete. Take a five-token vocabulary with

\[p = (0.50,\; 0.25,\; 0.15,\; 0.07,\; 0.03), \qquad q = (0.30,\; 0.30,\; 0.20,\; 0.10,\; 0.10).\]

The draft over-weights tokens 1 through 4 and under-weights token 0. If the draft proposes token 0, the acceptance probability is \(\min(1, 0.5/0.3) = 1\), so it is always kept. If it proposes token 4, the acceptance probability is \(0.03/0.10 = 0.3\), so it is usually rejected. The residual is \(\max(0, p - q) = (0.20, 0, 0, 0, 0)\), which normalizes to \((1, 0, 0, 0, 0)\). So in this example, whenever a rejection happens, the replacement is token 0, the one token the draft did not propose often enough. The two corrections push in opposite directions and balance exactly, which the next section shows in general.

Why the output has the target’s distribution

Fix one position and condition on everything before it. Let \(\tilde{x}\) denote the token that the procedure emits there, either an accepted draft token or the replacement. We will show that \(\Pr[\tilde{x} = x] = p(x)\) for every token \(x\).

There are two ways to emit \(x\). The first is that the draft proposes \(x\) and it is accepted:

\[\Pr[\text{propose } x \text{ and accept}] = q(x)\,\min\!\Big(1, \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\Big) = \min\big(p(x), q(x)\big).\]

The second is that a rejection occurs and the residual distribution produces \(x\). The total probability of a rejection, which we call \(\rho\), is

\[\rho = 1 - \sum_y \min\big(p(y), q(y)\big) = \sum_y \big(p(y) - \min(p(y), q(y))\big) = \sum_y \max\big(0, p(y) - q(y)\big).\]

That is exactly the normalizing constant of the residual distribution, so \(\rho > 0\) whenever a rejection can happen. (If \(p = q\), no rejection ever occurs and the residual is never needed.) So

\[\Pr[\text{reject and then emit } x] = \rho \cdot \frac{\max(0, p(x) - q(x))}{\rho} = \max\big(0, p(x) - q(x)\big).\]

Adding the two cases,

\[\Pr[\tilde{x} = x] = \min\big(p(x), q(x)\big) + \max\big(0, p(x) - q(x)\big) = p(x).\]

The last equality holds because for any two numbers \(a\) and \(b\), \(\min(a, b) + \max(0, a - b) = a\). This is the same acceptance-and-correction trick that appears in classical rejection sampling, adapted so that a rejected proposal is replaced by a draw from the leftover mass instead of being retried.

The argument above is for a single position. For a whole sequence, apply it position by position: once a token has been emitted, the next step is the same one-position problem with a longer context. The first emitted token has distribution \(p(\cdot \mid \text{context})\) by the result above. Given that token, whatever route produced it, the next emitted token is again handled by the same procedure with the longer context: if the first token was an accepted draft token, the round continues and tests the next draft token against \(p\) for the extended context; if it was a replacement, the round ends and a new one starts from that extended context. Either way the second token has distribution \(p(\cdot \mid \text{context}, \text{first token})\). By the chain rule of probability, the product of these conditionals is the target’s distribution over the whole sequence [1].

Two remarks on the scope of this guarantee. It holds for any draft distribution \(q\), even a terrible one. A poor draft does not change what is generated, only how fast. The requirement is about which distributions enter the acceptance test. \(p\) must be the distribution you want the output to follow, so if you sample with temperature, top-\(k\), or nucleus filtering, apply those settings to the target’s logits first. \(q\) must be exactly the distribution the draft token was sampled from, whatever settings produced it. Applying the same filters to the draft is a good idea because it raises the acceptance rate, but exactness does not depend on it.

How many tokens per round

The expected number of tokens per round determines the speedup, so let us compute it. Define the acceptance rate

\[\alpha = \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_x \min\big(p(x), q(x)\big)\Big],\]

which is the probability that a draft token is accepted. At a single position the acceptance probability equals \(1 - \mathrm{TV}(p, q)\), where TV is the total variation distance between the two distributions, so \(\alpha\) is one minus the average TV distance. In the example above, \(\alpha = 0.3 + 0.25 + 0.15 + 0.07 + 0.03 = 0.8\).

If we treat the acceptance of each draft token as an independent event with probability \(\alpha\), the first \(i\) draft tokens are all accepted with probability \(\alpha^i\). A round always emits one token (the replacement or the bonus) plus one for each accepted draft token before the first rejection, so

\[\mathbb{E}[\text{tokens per round}] = 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{\gamma} \alpha^i = \frac{1 - \alpha^{\gamma + 1}}{1 - \alpha}.\]

This matches Eq. 1 in Leviathan et al. [1]. Real acceptance rates vary from position to position, so the formula is an approximation for real models and exact when the acceptance probability is the same everywhere.

Now let the draft model be cheaper to run than the target by a factor \(c\), meaning that one draft step costs \(c\) times as much as one target step. A round costs \(\gamma c + 1\) target-step equivalents, assuming that scoring \(\gamma + 1\) positions costs the same as scoring one, which is the memory-bound assumption from the first section. The expected speedup over ordinary decoding is therefore

\[\text{speedup} = \frac{1 - \alpha^{\gamma + 1}}{(1 - \alpha)(\gamma c + 1)},\]

which is the wall-clock improvement factor of Leviathan et al. [1]. The formula shows the trade-off in choosing \(\gamma\). A longer draft raises the numerator, but with diminishing returns because \(\alpha^{\gamma+1}\) shrinks geometrically (slowly when \(\alpha\) is close to 1), while the denominator grows linearly. There is an optimal \(\gamma\) for each pair \((\alpha, c)\).

An implementation to test the claims

We will implement the algorithm for toy models whose next-token distributions we can write down exactly, so that we can compare the output of speculative decoding with the true distribution rather than with another sample. The “models” are functions from a context to a probability vector. The same code would work with real models if p_fn and q_fn called them.

The core function follows the five steps above. The buggy flag switches the repair step to a common mistake, resampling from \(p\) instead of the residual, so that we can see what an incorrect implementation looks like.

import numpy as np

def softmax(z):
    z = z - z.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)

def sample(p, rng):
    """Draw one index from the probability vector p."""
    return min(int(np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(p), rng.random())), len(p) - 1)

def residual(p, q):
    """The distribution norm(max(0, p - q)) used after a rejection."""
    r = np.maximum(p - q, 0.0)
    return r / r.sum()

def speculative_round(prefix, p_fn, q_fn, gamma, rng, buggy=False):
    """One draft-and-verify round. Returns the tokens emitted (between 1 and gamma + 1)."""
    # 1. The draft model proposes gamma tokens, one at a time.
    ctx, drafts, q_dists = list(prefix), [], []
    for _ in range(gamma):
        q = q_fn(ctx)
        x = sample(q, rng)
        q_dists.append(q)
        drafts.append(x)
        ctx.append(x)
    # 2. The target model scores all gamma + 1 positions (one forward pass in a real system).
    p_dists = [p_fn(list(prefix) + drafts[:i]) for i in range(gamma + 1)]
    # 3. Verify the draft tokens from left to right.
    out = []
    for i, x in enumerate(drafts):
        p, q = p_dists[i], q_dists[i]
        if rng.random() < min(1.0, p[x] / q[x]):
            out.append(x)                                   # accept the draft token
        else:
            fix = p if buggy else residual(p, q)            # buggy variant: resample from p itself
            out.append(sample(fix, rng))                    # replacement token
            return out                                      # stop at the first rejection
    out.append(sample(p_dists[-1], rng))                    # every draft accepted: bonus token
    return out

Two small drivers: one for speculative generation of a fixed number of tokens, and one for ordinary sampling from the target to serve as the reference.

def generate(prefix, length, p_fn, q_fn, gamma, rng, buggy=False):
    """Speculative generation of `length` tokens. Returns (tokens, number of target passes)."""
    seq, rounds = list(prefix), 0
    while len(seq) - len(prefix) < length:
        seq += speculative_round(seq, p_fn, q_fn, gamma, rng, buggy)
        rounds += 1
    return seq[len(prefix):len(prefix) + length], rounds

def generate_plain(prefix, length, p_fn, rng):
    """Ordinary sampling from the target model, one token per step."""
    seq = list(prefix)
    for _ in range(length):
        seq.append(sample(p_fn(seq), rng))
    return seq[len(prefix):]

Test 1: one position

First the single-position claim. We use the five-token \(p\) and \(q\) from the worked example, run one round with \(\gamma = 1\) many times, and record the first token emitted. For comparison we also run the buggy variant, and compute its distribution analytically. Since a rejection then replaces the token with a sample from \(p\), the output probability would be \(\min(p, q) + \rho\, p\) with \(\rho = 1 - \alpha\).

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
p = np.array([0.50, 0.25, 0.15, 0.07, 0.03])      # target distribution
q = np.array([0.30, 0.30, 0.20, 0.10, 0.10])      # draft distribution
alpha = np.minimum(p, q).sum()                    # acceptance probability
p_fn, q_fn = (lambda ctx: p), (lambda ctx: q)     # same distributions at every position

print("alpha =", round(alpha, 3))
print("residual after a rejection:", np.round(residual(p, q), 3))
N = 200_000
print("target                  ", p)
freqs = {}
for name, buggy in [("correct", False), ("resample from p", True)]:
    counts = np.zeros(len(p))
    for _ in range(N):
        counts[speculative_round([], p_fn, q_fn, 1, rng, buggy)[0]] += 1
    freq = counts / N
    freqs[name] = freq
    print(f"{name:24s}", np.round(freq, 4), f" TV = {0.5 * np.abs(freq - p).sum():.4f}")
print("buggy, exact calculation ", np.round(np.minimum(p, q) + (1 - alpha) * p, 4))

alpha = 0.8

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams.update({"font.size": 10, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.7))
x, w = np.arange(len(p)), 0.2
ax.bar(x - 1.5 * w, p, w, color="#08519c", label="target p")
ax.bar(x - 0.5 * w, q, w, color="#bdbdbd", label="draft q")

The correct implementation reproduces \(p\) to within sampling noise (the total variation distance is 0.0004 here; with 200,000 draws, distances of a few thousandths would also be unremarkable). The buggy variant is off by 0.10 in total variation, and its empirical frequencies agree with the exact calculation, so the discrepancy is real and not noise. The error is also easy to miss in casual testing: the buggy output still looks like a sensible distribution, and it is closer to \(p\) than \(q\) is. Only comparing against the exact target reveals it.

Test 2: tokens per round

Next the formula for the expected number of tokens per round. With the same fixed \(p\) and \(q\), the acceptance probability is identical at every position, which is the case where the formula is exact.

print("gamma   simulated   formula")
simulated = {}
for gamma in [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8]:
    emitted = [len(speculative_round([], p_fn, q_fn, gamma, rng)) for _ in range(50_000)]
    simulated[gamma] = np.mean(emitted)
    formula = (1 - alpha ** (gamma + 1)) / (1 - alpha)
    print(f"{gamma:5d}   {np.mean(emitted):9.3f}   {formula:7.3f}")

gamma   simulated   formula
    1       1.800     1.800
    2       2.438     2.440
    3       2.956     2.952
    4       3.346     3.362
    6       3.965     3.951
    8       4.342     4.329

gs = np.arange(1, 11)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
ax.plot(gs, (1 - alpha ** (gs + 1)) / (1 - alpha), color="#08519c", lw=2, label="formula")
ax.plot(list(simulated), list(simulated.values()), "o", color="#d95f02", ms=7, label="simulation")
ax.set_xlabel("draft tokens per round, gamma"); ax.set_ylabel("tokens emitted per round"); ax.legend(frameon=False)

The simulated averages follow the formula closely. The small differences are sampling error from 50,000 rounds per row. Note how the gains flatten: going from \(\gamma = 4\) to \(\gamma = 8\) doubles the draft work but adds only about one extra token per round.

Test 3: whole sequences with context-dependent models

The last test is the strongest. Here the models condition on the previous token, so the distribution at each position depends on what came before, and the draft is a noisy version of the target. We generate sequences of three tokens, which gives 64 possible outcomes. Because the target is a small Markov chain, the exact probability of each sequence is a product of table entries. We compare the empirical frequencies of speculative decoding, ordinary sampling, and the buggy variant against those exact probabilities with a chi-square statistic, which should land near the number of degrees of freedom (63) if the samples really follow the exact distribution.

import itertools
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
V, L, N = 4, 3, 100_000
logits = rng.normal(size=(V, V)) * 1.5
P = softmax(logits)                                   # target: row = previous token
Q = softmax(logits + rng.normal(size=(V, V)) * 0.8)   # draft: related to the target but imperfect
p_fn, q_fn = (lambda ctx: P[ctx[-1]]), (lambda ctx: Q[ctx[-1]])
start = [0]

seqs = list(itertools.product(range(V), repeat=L))
index = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(seqs)}
exact = np.array([P[start[0], s[0]] * P[s[0], s[1]] * P[s[1], s[2]] for s in seqs])

def empirical(make_sequence):
    counts = np.zeros(len(seqs))
    for _ in range(N):
        counts[index[tuple(make_sequence())]] += 1
    return counts / N

runs = {
    "ordinary sampling": empirical(lambda: generate_plain(start, L, p_fn, rng)),
    "speculative":       empirical(lambda: generate(start, L, p_fn, q_fn, 4, rng)[0]),
    "buggy variant":     empirical(lambda: generate(start, L, p_fn, q_fn, 4, rng, buggy=True)[0]),
}
dof = len(seqs) - 1
print(f"{len(seqs)} possible sequences; chi-square should be near {dof} (give or take {(2 * dof) ** 0.5:.0f})")
for name, freq in runs.items():
    chi2 = N * ((freq - exact) ** 2 / exact).sum()
    print(f"{name:18s} chi-square = {chi2:8.1f}   TV distance = {0.5 * np.abs(freq - exact).sum():.4f}")

64 possible sequences; chi-square should be near 63 (give or take 11)
ordinary sampling  chi-square =     63.9   TV distance = 0.0089
speculative        chi-square =     55.6   TV distance = 0.0073
buggy variant      chi-square =  12100.3   TV distance = 0.1319

Ordinary sampling and speculative decoding both land within the expected range of 63 (give or take about 11), so neither can be distinguished from the exact target distribution at this sample size. (One of the 64 sequences has an expected count of about 3.4, a little under the usual rule of thumb of 5 for the chi-square approximation, so treat the statistic as a rough guide. The gap to the buggy variant is far too large for that to matter.) The buggy variant gives a statistic of about 12,000. A test of this kind is worth keeping around when you build a speculative decoding system: it catches the mistakes that make output slightly wrong but still fluent.

This test supports the correctness argument but does not replace it. A chi-square test cannot prove equality, and with finite samples it can only fail to find a difference. The proof in the earlier section is what establishes exactness.

What the speedup formula predicts

Finally, a table of the speedup formula for a few choices of acceptance rate \(\alpha\) and relative draft cost \(c\). These numbers come from the formula, not from timing a real system.

def improvement(alpha, gamma, c):
    """Expected wall-clock speedup when one draft step costs c target steps."""
    return (1 - alpha ** (gamma + 1)) / ((1 - alpha) * (gamma * c + 1))

gammas = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10]
print("gamma            " + "".join(f"{g:6d}" for g in gammas))
for c in (0.02, 0.1):
    for a in (0.6, 0.8, 0.9):
        print(f"c={c:<4} alpha={a}  " + "".join(f"{improvement(a, g, c):6.2f}" for g in gammas))

With a cheap draft (\(c = 0.02\)) and a high acceptance rate (\(\alpha = 0.9\)), the model predicts more than a 5× gain at \(\gamma = 8\) to \(10\). With a draft that costs a tenth of the target and an acceptance rate of 0.6, the best case is under 1.7×, and the gain shrinks to 1.25× if \(\gamma\) is pushed to 10. The two quantities that matter, \(\alpha\) and \(c\), pull against each other in practice: a bigger draft model agrees with the target more often but costs more to run.

What the model leaves out

The formula describes the ideal case, and real deployments differ from it in several ways.

  • Extra computation. Speculative decoding performs more total arithmetic than ordinary decoding, since rejected draft tokens are computed and thrown away, and the target scores positions that may not be used. It trades spare compute for lower latency. When a server is already compute-bound, for instance when it batches many requests together, the benefit shrinks or disappears.
  • The memory-bound assumption. Scoring \(\gamma + 1\) positions at the price of one only holds while the pass is limited by memory traffic. For long drafts, large batches, or hardware with high bandwidth relative to its arithmetic throughput, the verification pass starts to cost more.
  • Acceptance varies. Text that is easy to predict, such as boilerplate, code syntax, or repetition of earlier content, gets high acceptance rates. Open-ended text gets lower ones. The measured speedup therefore depends on the task, not just on the model pair.
  • The draft must share the vocabulary. The acceptance ratio compares \(p(x)\) with \(q(x)\) for the same token \(x\), so the two models need the same tokenizer. A small model from the same family is the usual choice.
  • Overheads. Real systems must also manage the key-value caches of both models and roll back the cache entries for rejected tokens, and these implementation costs reduce the ideal gain.

Variations and related work

The accept-and-correct rule is general, and much of the research since the original papers concerns where the draft tokens come from. Not every method below keeps the exact-distribution guarantee in every mode, so check each one’s sampling procedure. EAGLE and SpecInfer are designed to preserve the target distribution. Medusa’s default acceptance rule for sampled generation is a relaxed criterion that trades exactness for acceptance rate, and exactness holds there for greedy decoding or when using a rejection-sampling variant. Some systems train extra prediction heads on the target model itself so that no separate draft model is needed, as in Medusa [4]. Others draft in the target’s feature space, as in EAGLE [5], which improves the acceptance rate. Tree-based approaches such as SpecInfer [6] verify several candidate continuations at once by arranging them in a tree and using a suitable attention mask. Earlier ideas such as blockwise parallel decoding [7] were already exploring parallel verification of multiple tokens, though without the exact-distribution guarantee in this form.

Two further points are worth knowing. With greedy decoding (temperature zero) the target distribution puts all of its mass on one token, so the rule reduces to a simple check: keep a draft token if and only if it is the target’s most likely token. And the guarantee is about distributions, not about identical bits. Batched or reshaped computation can change floating-point rounding, so in rare near-ties a greedy run might differ in a token or two from a non-speculative run on the same hardware, even though the procedure is exact in exact arithmetic.

Common implementation errors

  • Resampling from \(p\) instead of the residual. The most common mistake, and the one tested above. The output looks fine and is wrong.
  • Forgetting to renormalize the residual. \(\max(0, p - q)\) sums to the rejection probability \(\rho\), not to 1.
  • A missed optimization: dropping the bonus token. When all drafts are accepted, the target has already computed \(p_{\gamma+1}\). Ignoring it is still correct, but it wastes one free token per fully accepted round.
  • Wrong distributions in the ratio. The ratio must use the processed target distribution you actually want to sample from (after temperature, top-\(k\), or top-\(p\)) as \(p\), and the exact distribution the draft token was sampled from as \(q\). Using unprocessed target probabilities, or a \(q\) that differs from the one used for sampling, breaks the guarantee.
  • Cache bookkeeping. After a rejection, the key-value entries for the discarded tokens must be removed from both models, or later tokens will attend to text that was never emitted.

Where to go next

If you want to try this on real models, the Hugging Face transformers library supports assisted generation with a separate draft model, and serving frameworks such as vLLM include speculative decoding. The two original papers [1] [2] are both short and readable, and the proof above follows the first. Chen et al. also analyze the algorithm for a fixed number of draft tokens and report results on a 70-billion-parameter model.

References

  1. Y. Leviathan, M. Kalman, and Y. Matias. “Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding.” ICML, 2023. arXiv:2211.17192
  2. C. Chen, S. Borgeaud, G. Irving, J.-B. Lespiau, L. Sifre, and J. Jumper. “Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling.” 2023. arXiv:2302.01318
  3. S. Williams, A. Waterman, and D. Patterson. “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures.” Communications of the ACM, 52(4):65–76, 2009.
  4. T. Cai, Y. Li, Z. Geng, H. Peng, J. D. Lee, D. Chen, and T. Dao. “Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads.” ICML, 2024. arXiv:2401.10774
  5. Y. Li, F. Wei, C. Zhang, and H. Zhang. “EAGLE: Speculative Sampling Requires Rethinking Feature Uncertainty.” ICML, 2024. arXiv:2401.15077
  6. X. Miao et al. “SpecInfer: Accelerating Large Language Model Serving with Tree-based Speculative Inference and Verification.” ASPLOS, 2024. arXiv:2305.09781
  7. M. Stern, N. Shazeer, and J. Uszkoreit. “Blockwise Parallel Decoding for Deep Autoregressive Models.” NeurIPS, 2018. arXiv:1811.03115

entry.title: Vision-Language Models from Scratch: Teaching a Language Model to See

link.title: Vision-Language Models from Scratch: Teaching a Language Model to See

entry.content:
A language model reads and writes text. A vision-language model, or VLM, also looks at images. Ask it what is in a photo, what a chart says, or whether a sign is in focus, and it answers in words. Over the last few years this has gone from a research curiosity to a standard feature of large models, and the design behind most of them is simpler than it looks.

The central idea is to turn an image into a short sequence of vectors that a language model can read as if they were word embeddings. After that, the language model does what it always does: it predicts the next token. In this post we build a small version of this recipe from scratch and train it on a toy world of colored shapes, where we can check every answer. We then use it for something relevant to the practical cost of VLMs: measuring what happens when we drop most of the visual tokens before the language model sees them.

You should be comfortable with the transformer, which we build in an earlier post, and with the idea of a language model, covered in the post on how LLMs work.

Two families of vision-language models

There are two main ways to connect images and text, and it helps to separate them early.

Contrastive models such as CLIP [1] train an image encoder and a text encoder together so that a picture and its caption land close to each other in a shared embedding space, and mismatched pairs land far apart. They do not generate text. They are used to score how well an image matches a piece of text, which gives zero-shot classification (compare an image with the text “a photo of a dog” and “a photo of a cat” and pick the closer one) and image search. They are also a common source of the image encoder in the second family.

Generative models such as LLaVA [2] take images as input and produce text. A vision encoder turns the image into a set of feature vectors, a small projector maps those vectors into the language model’s embedding space, and the language model reads them as a prefix before the question and then writes the answer. Training uses the usual next-token loss on the answer. Other designs feed the image into the language model through cross-attention layers instead of as a prefix, as in Flamingo [3], or compress the image features into a fixed number of learned query vectors first, as in BLIP-2 [4].

This post builds the second family in its simplest form, the prefix design, and shows the contrastive loss in a short snippet so that you can see how the two relate.

A toy world

Real VLMs are trained on hundreds of millions of image-text pairs, which is not something we can do on a laptop. Instead we build a world small enough to train in minutes but structured enough to ask real questions about. Each image is \(48 \times 48\) pixels with a \(3 \times 3\) grid of cells. It contains one to three shapes, each of a different kind (circle, square, triangle), each in its own cell, and each in one of four colors. A small random jitter moves each shape inside its cell, so no two images are pixel-identical.

For every image we generate text tasks. A caption lists the shapes in reading order. A count question asks how many shapes there are. A color question asks what color a named shape is. A where question asks which of nine cells a named shape is in. An existence question asks whether a shape is present, with about half of the answers being no. The scene description, the rendering, and the tasks are all in the code:

import math, os, time
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams.update({"font.size": 11, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
os.makedirs("figures", exist_ok=True)
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu"

COLORS = {"red": (220, 40, 40), "green": (40, 160, 60), "blue": (50, 90, 220), "yellow": (240, 200, 30)}
SHAPES = ["circle", "square", "triangle"]
CELL_NAMES = ["top left", "top middle", "top right", "middle left", "center", "middle right",
              "bottom left", "bottom middle", "bottom right"]
CELL, SIZE = 16, 48                                        # a 3x3 grid of 16-pixel cells -> a 48x48 image

def shape_mask(kind, size=11):
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[:size, :size]
    c = (size - 1) / 2
    if kind == "circle":
        return (yy - c) ** 2 + (xx - c) ** 2 <= (size / 2) ** 2
    if kind == "square":
        return np.ones((size, size), dtype=bool)
    return np.abs(xx - c) <= yy * c / (size - 1)           # triangle pointing up

MASKS = {k: shape_mask(k) for k in SHAPES}

def make_scene(rng):
    """1-3 shapes of different kinds, each in its own cell of the 3x3 grid, in random colors."""
    n = int(rng.integers(1, 4))
    kinds = rng.permutation(SHAPES)[:n]
    cells = rng.choice(9, size=n, replace=False)
    colors = rng.choice(list(COLORS), size=n)
    return sorted(zip(cells.tolist(), kinds.tolist(), colors.tolist()))     # reading order: row by row

def render(scene, rng):
    img = np.full((SIZE, SIZE, 3), 255, dtype=np.uint8)
    for cell, kind, color in scene:
        r, c = divmod(cell, 3)
        dy, dx = rng.integers(0, 5, size=2)               # small random offset inside the cell
        y0, x0 = r * CELL + dy, c * CELL + dx
        m = MASKS[kind]
        img[y0:y0 + m.shape[0], x0:x0 + m.shape[1]][m] = COLORS[color]
    return img

def caption(scene):
    parts = [f"a {color} {kind}" for _, kind, color in scene]
    return (" , ".join(parts[:-1]) + " and " + parts[-1] if len(parts) > 1 else parts[0]) + " ."

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
demo = [make_scene(rng) for _ in range(3)]
for s in demo:
    print(caption(s))

a yellow triangle , a yellow square and a blue circle .
a blue circle and a yellow triangle .
a green triangle .

NUMBER_WORDS = ["one", "two", "three"]

def make_examples(scene, rng):
    """Text tasks for one scene, as (task, prompt, answer) triples of space-separated words."""
    kinds = {k: (cell, color) for cell, k, color in scene}
    present = list(kinds)
    absent = [k for k in SHAPES if k not in kinds]
    ex = [("caption", "<cap>", caption(scene)),
          ("count", "how many shapes ?", NUMBER_WORDS[len(scene) - 1])]
    k = present[rng.integers(len(present))]
    ex.append(("color", f"what color is the {k} ?", kinds[k][1]))
    k = present[rng.integers(len(present))]
    ex.append(("where", f"where is the {k} ?", CELL_NAMES[kinds[k][0]]))
    ex.append(("exist", f"is there a {present[rng.integers(len(present))]} ?", "yes"))
    if absent:
        ex.append(("exist", f"is there a {absent[rng.integers(len(absent))]} ?", "no"))
    else:
        ex.append(("exist", f"is there a {present[rng.integers(len(present))]} ?", "yes"))
    return ex

words = sorted({w for k in SHAPES for w in [k]} | set(COLORS) | set(CELL_NAMES[i].split()[j] for i in range(9) for j in range(len(CELL_NAMES[i].split())))
               | set(NUMBER_WORDS) | {"yes", "no", "a", "and", ",", ".", "?", "<cap>", "how", "many", "shapes", "what",
                                       "color", "is", "the", "there", "where"})
vocab = ["<pad>", "<eos>"] + words
stoi = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(vocab)}
print(f"vocabulary: {len(vocab)} words")

TEXT_LEN = 24
def encode_example(prompt, answer):
    p, a = prompt.split(), answer.split()
    ids = [stoi[w] for w in p + a] + [stoi["<eos>"]]
    mask = [0] * len(p) + [1] * (len(a) + 1)              # the loss is computed on the answer only
    pad = TEXT_LEN - len(ids)
    return ids + [0] * pad, mask + [0] * pad

def build_split(n_scenes, seed):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    images, ids, masks, tasks, scene_idx = [], [], [], [], []
    for s in range(n_scenes):
        scene = make_scene(rng)
        images.append(render(scene, rng))
        for task, prompt, answer in make_examples(scene, rng):
            i, m = encode_example(prompt, answer)
            ids.append(i); masks.append(m); tasks.append(task); scene_idx.append(s)
    return (torch.tensor(np.stack(images)).permute(0, 3, 1, 2).contiguous(),
            torch.tensor(ids), torch.tensor(masks), np.array(tasks), torch.tensor(scene_idx))

train = build_split(20_000, seed=1)
test = build_split(2_000, seed=2)
print("train:", len(train[0]), "scenes,", len(train[1]), "text examples;  test:", len(test[0]), "scenes,", len(test[1]), "text examples")
print("example:", " ".join(vocab[i] for i in train[1][1] if i != 0))

vocabulary: 35 words
train: 20000 scenes, 120000 text examples;  test: 2000 scenes, 12000 text examples
example: how many shapes ? two <eos>

The vocabulary is just 35 words. The data set has 20,000 training scenes with six text examples each, and 2,000 held-out test scenes. A few training images and their captions:

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(11, 5.6))
for ax, i in zip(axes.ravel(), range(8)):
    ax.imshow(train[0][i].permute(1, 2, 0)); ax.axis("off")
    cap = " ".join(vocab[j] for j in train[1][6 * i].tolist() if j > 1 and j != stoi["<cap>"])
    ax.set_title(cap.replace(" ,", ",").replace(" .", "."), fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig("figures/vlm_data.png", dpi=170, bbox_inches="tight")

The model

The model has three parts, and each is small.

The vision encoder is a miniature vision transformer [5]. It cuts the image into \(8 \times 8\) pixel patches, giving a grid of \(6 \times 6 = 36\) patches. A single convolution with stride 8 turns each patch into a vector, which is the same as applying one shared linear map to every flattened patch. A learned position embedding is added so that the model knows where each patch came from, and two transformer blocks let the patches exchange information. The attention here is not causal: every patch can look at every other. The output is 36 vectors of width 64.

The projector is a two-layer network that maps each 64-dimensional visual vector into the 128-dimensional embedding space of the language model. In LLaVA the first version of this was a single linear layer, and a two-layer MLP was found to work better [6]. The projector is where the visual world is translated into the language model’s input space, and it is typically the only part that is trained from scratch when the encoder and the language model are both pretrained.

The language model is a small decoder-only transformer with causal attention, like the one in the transformer post. Its input sequence is the 36 projected visual tokens followed by the text tokens of the question and, during training, the answer. It uses one positional table for the whole sequence, so that visual tokens occupy positions 0 to 35, and text begins at position 36.

During training we compute the usual next-token cross-entropy but only on the answer tokens, not on the question. The model is not being trained to predict questions. The code makes this explicit with a loss mask.

class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, heads, causal):
        super().__init__()
        self.heads, self.causal = heads, causal
        self.ln1, self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(d), nn.LayerNorm(d)
        self.qkv, self.proj = nn.Linear(d, 3 * d), nn.Linear(d, d)
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 4 * d), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(4 * d, d))
    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(self.ln1(x)).view(B, T, 3, self.heads, C // self.heads).permute(2, 0, 3, 1, 4)
        y = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=self.causal)    # (B, H, T, dh)
        x = x + self.proj(y.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, C))
        return x + self.mlp(self.ln2(x))

class VisionEncoder(nn.Module):
    """A small ViT: cut the image into 8x8 patches, embed them, let them attend to each other."""
    def __init__(self, d=64, layers=2, patch=8):
        super().__init__()
        self.embed = nn.Conv2d(3, d, patch, stride=patch)                   # one linear map per patch
        self.pos = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1, (SIZE // patch) ** 2, d))
        nn.init.normal_(self.pos, std=0.02)
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([Block(d, 4, causal=False) for _ in range(layers)])
        self.ln = nn.LayerNorm(d)
    def forward(self, img):
        x = self.embed(img.float() / 127.5 - 1).flatten(2).transpose(1, 2) + self.pos   # (B, 36, d)
        for b in self.blocks:
            x = b(x)
        return self.ln(x)

class TinyVLM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, d_vis=64, d=128, layers=4, n_patches=36):
        super().__init__()
        self.n_patches = n_patches
        self.vision = VisionEncoder(d_vis)
        self.projector = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d_vis, d), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(d, d))   # vision space -> language space
        self.tok = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d)
        self.pos = nn.Embedding(n_patches + TEXT_LEN, d)
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([Block(d, 4, causal=True) for _ in range(layers)])
        self.ln = nn.LayerNorm(d)
        self.head = nn.Linear(d, vocab_size, bias=False)
        self.head.weight = self.tok.weight
        for emb in (self.tok, self.pos):                                     # small initial embeddings -> near-uniform first predictions
            nn.init.normal_(emb.weight, std=0.02)

    def visual_tokens(self, img):
        return self.projector(self.vision(img))                              # (B, 36, d)

    def forward(self, text, vis=None, keep=None):
        """text: (B, T) word ids. vis: (B, k, d) visual tokens, with their original patch indices in keep (B, k)."""
        B, T = text.shape
        if keep is None:
            keep = torch.arange(self.n_patches, device=text.device).expand(B, -1)
        k = vis.size(1)
        text_pos = self.n_patches + torch.arange(T, device=text.device)
        x = torch.cat([vis + self.pos(keep), self.tok(text) + self.pos(text_pos)], dim=1)
        for b in self.blocks:
            x = b(x)
        return self.head(self.ln(x[:, k:]))                                  # logits at the text positions

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = TinyVLM(len(vocab)).to(device)
n_vis = sum(p.numel() for p in model.vision.parameters()) + sum(p.numel() for p in model.projector.parameters())
print(f"parameters: {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()):,} "
      f"(vision encoder + projector: {n_vis:,}; language model: {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) - n_vis:,})")

parameters: 945,088 (vision encoder + projector: 139,584; language model: 805,504)

The whole model has 945,088 parameters. Of those, 139,584 belong to the vision encoder and projector, and 805,504 to the language model.

One detail worth pointing out is that each visual token carries its original patch index through to the positional lookup. This is not needed for the baseline, where all 36 tokens are present in order. It becomes important in the last experiment, where we remove some tokens and need the remaining ones to keep their identity.

Training

We train the vision encoder, the projector, and the language model together, from random initialization, for 6,000 steps with AdamW and a one-cycle learning rate schedule. Every step takes a batch of 128 text examples, looks up the image for each, and computes the loss on the answer tokens.

imgs_tr, ids_tr, mask_tr, tasks_tr, sidx_tr = [t.to(device) if torch.is_tensor(t) else t for t in train]
steps, batch_size, lr = 6000, 128, 1e-3
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=0.01, betas=(0.9, 0.95))
sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.OneCycleLR(opt, max_lr=lr, total_steps=steps, pct_start=0.05)
history, start = [], time.time()
torch.manual_seed(0)
for step in range(1, steps + 1):
    idx = torch.randint(len(ids_tr), (batch_size,), device=device)
    text, mask = ids_tr[idx], mask_tr[idx]
    vis = model.visual_tokens(imgs_tr[sidx_tr[idx]])
    logits = model(text[:, :-1], vis)                                        # predict word j+1 from words up to j
    loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, logits.size(-1)), text[:, 1:].reshape(-1), reduction="none")
    loss = (loss * mask[:, 1:].reshape(-1)).sum() / mask[:, 1:].sum()        # average over answer tokens only
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0); opt.step(); sched.step()
    history.append(loss.item())
    if step in (1, 250, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 6000):
        print(f"step {step:5d} | loss {np.mean(history[-50:]):.4f} | {time.time() - start:4.0f}s")

step     1 | loss 3.6353 |    2s
step   250 | loss 0.4845 |   52s
step   500 | loss 0.3046 |  111s
step  1000 | loss 0.1183 |  227s
step  2000 | loss 0.0274 |  462s
step  4000 | loss 0.0005 |  846s
step  6000 | loss 0.0000 | 1134s

The loss starts near \(\ln 35 \approx 3.6\), which is what a uniform guess over the vocabulary would give, falls quickly during the first thousand steps, and ends at essentially zero.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.4))
sm = np.convolve(history, np.ones(25) / 25, mode="valid")
ax.plot(history, color="#c6dbef", lw=0.6); ax.plot(np.arange(len(sm)) + 12, sm, color="#08519c", lw=1.8)
ax.set_xlabel("training step"); ax.set_ylabel("answer-token loss"); ax.set_yscale("log")
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig("figures/vlm_loss.png", dpi=170, bbox_inches="tight")

Does it work?

We evaluate on the 2,000 held-out scenes with greedy decoding: the model is given an image and a question, and writes the most likely next word repeatedly until it emits an end-of-sequence token. An answer counts as correct only if the whole generated string matches the target exactly. A caption is correct only if every word is right.

imgs_te, ids_te, mask_te, tasks_te, sidx_te = [t.to(device) if torch.is_tensor(t) else t for t in test]

@torch.no_grad()
def answer(prompt_ids, vis, keep=None, max_new=14):
    """Greedy decoding: append the most likely word until every sequence has produced <eos>."""
    text = prompt_ids
    done = torch.zeros(len(text), dtype=torch.bool, device=device)
    out = []
    for _ in range(max_new):
        nxt = model(text, vis, keep)[:, -1].argmax(-1)
        nxt = torch.where(done, torch.zeros_like(nxt), nxt)
        out.append(nxt); text = torch.cat([text, nxt[:, None]], dim=1)
        done |= nxt == stoi["<eos>"]
        if done.all():
            break
    return torch.stack(out, dim=1)

def accuracy_by_task(vis_fn=None, bs=500):
    """Exact-match accuracy per task on the test set. vis_fn(images) -> (visual tokens, patch indices)."""
    model.eval()
    results = {}
    for task in ["caption", "count", "color", "where", "exist"]:
        rows = torch.tensor(np.where(tasks_te == task)[0], device=device)
        correct = 0
        for i in range(0, len(rows), bs):
            r = rows[i:i + bs]
            text, mask = ids_te[r], mask_te[r]
            n_prompt = int(mask[0].nonzero()[0])                  # the answer starts where the loss mask turns on
            vis, keep = vis_fn(imgs_te[sidx_te[r]]) if vis_fn else (model.visual_tokens(imgs_te[sidx_te[r]]), None)
            pred = answer(text[:, :n_prompt], vis, keep)
            gold = text[:, n_prompt:n_prompt + pred.size(1)] * mask[:, n_prompt:n_prompt + pred.size(1)]
            correct += (pred == gold).all(dim=1).sum().item()
        results[task] = correct / len(rows)
    model.train()
    return results

with torch.no_grad():
    base = accuracy_by_task()
print("task      exact-match accuracy on held-out scenes")
for k, v in base.items():
    print(f"{k:8s}  {100 * v:5.1f}%")

task      exact-match accuracy on held-out scenes
caption   100.0%
count     100.0%
color     100.0%
where     100.0%
exist     100.0%

Perfect scores on every task. That deserves some suspicion before celebration, so let us look at what the number does and does not mean. First, this is a very easy world: the shapes are flat colors on a white background, the grid is regular, and the model is trained on 120,000 examples of a language with 35 words. A model of this size is expected to learn it. The point of the test is to show that the pipeline works, not that the model is capable. Second, the held-out scenes are new images, but many of the underlying layouts and color combinations appear in the training set in other jitter positions, so the test measures generalization to new pixel arrangements and not to new concepts. A harder test, such as withholding certain color and shape combinations during training, would be more demanding, and is a good exercise at the end.

What we can check is whether the model actually uses the image. The control is to give each question the image of a different scene. If the model were answering from the text alone, using the statistics of questions and answers, accuracy would not change. If it reads the image, accuracy should fall to the level of guessing.

# Control: show the question with the image of a *different* scene. If the model really reads the image,
# its accuracy should fall to the level of an educated guess.
def shuffled_vis(images):
    g = torch.Generator(device="cpu").manual_seed(0)
    perm = torch.randperm(len(images), generator=g).to(device)
    return model.visual_tokens(images[perm]), None

with torch.no_grad():
    blind = accuracy_by_task(shuffled_vis)
chance = {"caption": None, "count": 1 / 3, "color": 1 / 4, "where": 1 / 9, "exist": 1 / 2}
print("task      with the image   shown a different image   guess-level accuracy")
for k in base:
    ch = f"{100 * chance[k]:.0f}%" if chance[k] else "—"
    print(f"{k:8s}  {100 * base[k]:8.1f}%      {100 * blind[k]:8.1f}%                 {ch}")

task      with the image   shown a different image   guess-level accuracy
caption      100.0%           1.4%                 —
count        100.0%          33.0%                 33%
color        100.0%          25.3%                 25%
where        100.0%          10.5%                 11%
exist        100.0%          56.1%                 50%

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.4))
tasks_ = ["caption", "count", "color", "where", "exist"]
x = np.arange(len(tasks_))
ax.bar(x - 0.2, [100 * base[t] for t in tasks_], 0.4, color="#08519c", label="with the image")
ax.bar(x + 0.2, [100 * blind[t] for t in tasks_], 0.4, color="#d95f02", label="shown a different image")
ax.set_xticks(x); ax.set_xticklabels(tasks_); ax.set_ylabel("exact-match accuracy (%)"); ax.legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig("figures/vlm_blind.png", dpi=170, bbox_inches="tight")

The captions go from 100% to 1.4%, and the other tasks fall to roughly what random guessing gives: a third for counting three possible numbers, a quarter for four colors, a ninth for nine locations. The existence question falls to 56% instead of 50%, since the answer “yes” is a little more common than “no” in the data. The model answers from the image, and not from the question alone.

Here are six test images with the model’s answers to four of their questions.

model.eval()
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
picks = rng.choice(len(imgs_te), 6, replace=False)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(11, 6.6))
for ax, s in zip(axes.ravel(), picks):
    img = imgs_te[s:s + 1]
    rows = np.where(sidx_te.cpu().numpy() == s)[0]
    lines = []
    with torch.no_grad():
        vis = model.visual_tokens(img)
        for r in rows[:4]:
            text, mask = ids_te[r:r + 1], mask_te[r:r + 1]
            n_prompt = int(mask[0].nonzero()[0])
            pred = answer(text[:, :n_prompt], vis)[0].tolist()
            q = " ".join(vocab[i] for i in text[0, :n_prompt].tolist())
            a = " ".join(vocab[i] for i in pred if i > 1)
            lines.append(f"{q if q != '<cap>' else 'caption:'}  →  {a}")
    ax.imshow(img[0].permute(1, 2, 0).cpu()); ax.axis("off")
    ax.set_title("\n".join(l.replace(" ,", ",").replace(" .", ".").replace(" ?", "?") for l in lines), fontsize=8, loc="left")

model.train()
print("saved")

The cost of visual tokens

Now the part of this toy that carries over to real systems. In our model, the image becomes 36 tokens, so the language model’s input is the 36 visual tokens plus about ten text tokens. In a real VLM the number is much larger. LLaVA-1.5 uses a 336-pixel image cut into \(14 \times 14\) patches, which gives \(24 \times 24 = 576\) visual tokens for a single image [6]. Models that handle high-resolution images or several images, or video, can use thousands. Those tokens sit in the language model’s context for the whole answer. They add to the attention computation, they occupy space in the key-value cache, and the cache is already the main memory cost of generation, as discussed in the post on how LLMs work. In many VLMs, image tokens far outnumber the text tokens, so reducing them is attractive.

This motivates visual token pruning: keep only some of the visual tokens before, or inside, the language model. Published approaches include dropping tokens by attention score inside the language model, as in FastV [7], and merging similar tokens inside the vision encoder, as in ToMe [8]. Our toy lets us ask the basic question directly. How many of the 36 tokens does the model need, and which ones should we keep?

We try two rules, each keeping \(k\) of the 36 tokens. Random keeps a random subset. Content-based keeps the \(k\) patches with the most non-white pixels, a stand-in for a saliency score. In our images only a fraction of the patches contain any part of a shape: on the test set, an average of 7.9 of the 36, and at most 12. If the model only needs the patches with shapes in them, then the content rule should do very well down to about 12 tokens. The tokens keep their original position indices.

# Visual token pruning at inference time: keep only k of the 36 visual tokens before they enter the language model.
patch_mass = lambda images: (255 - images.float()).mean(dim=1).view(-1, 6, 8, 6, 8).mean(dim=(2, 4)).flatten(1)   # ink per patch

def make_pruner(k, mode):
    def fn(images):
        vis = model.visual_tokens(images)
        if k >= 36:
            return vis, None
        if mode == "random":
            scores = torch.rand(len(images), 36, device=device, generator=None)
        else:
            scores = patch_mass(images)                      # keep the patches that contain something
        keep = scores.topk(k, dim=1).indices.sort(dim=1).values
        return torch.gather(vis, 1, keep[:, :, None].expand(-1, -1, vis.size(2))), keep
    return fn

ks = [36, 24, 16, 12, 8, 6, 4, 2]
torch.manual_seed(0)
prune_results = {"random": [], "content-based": []}
with torch.no_grad():
    for k in ks:
        for mode, name in (("random", "random"), ("saliency", "content-based")):
            res = accuracy_by_task(make_pruner(k, mode))
            prune_results[name].append(res)
print("kept tokens   mean accuracy over count/color/where/exist:  random   content-based")
for i, k in enumerate(ks):
    r = np.mean([prune_results["random"][i][t] for t in ("count", "color", "where", "exist")])
    c = np.mean([prune_results["content-based"][i][t] for t in ("count", "color", "where", "exist")])
    print(f"{k:11d}   {100 * r:44.1f}%  {100 * c:9.1f}%")
ink = patch_mass(imgs_te).gt(1.0).sum(dim=1).float()
print(f"patches that contain any shape pixels: mean {ink.mean():.1f} of 36 (min {int(ink.min())}, max {int(ink.max())})")

Three things stand out. First, accuracy drops steeply for both rules as tokens are removed, far more than the arithmetic of “only 8 patches contain a shape” suggests. With 12 tokens kept, which is enough to cover every shape in every test image, the content rule gets 68.5% of questions right and random gets 66.5%. The model is evidently using the empty patches too. This is plausible: after two transformer layers of attention, each patch vector has mixed in information from the rest of the image, and a trained network can use some tokens as a place to keep global information, as has been observed in larger vision transformers [9]. Removing them removes information that the language model has learned to expect.

Second, content-based selection beats random for every budget here, which is what intuition suggests.

Third, and most important, the language model was never trained to see fewer tokens. Every training example had exactly 36. So these numbers describe how a model fails under a change it was not prepared for, not how well one could do. We can test that by fine-tuning the same model for 1,500 more steps, with a random number of tokens kept at each step, between 2 and 36.

# The model never saw a missing token during training. Fine-tune the same model for a short while with random
# visual-token dropout (a random number of tokens kept, between 2 and 36) so that the language model learns to cope.
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4, weight_decay=0.01, betas=(0.9, 0.95))
before_ft = {name: [dict(r) for r in rs] for name, rs in prune_results.items()}
torch.manual_seed(1)
ft_steps = 1500
for step in range(1, ft_steps + 1):
    idx = torch.randint(len(ids_tr), (batch_size,), device=device)
    text, mask = ids_tr[idx], mask_tr[idx]
    vis_all = model.visual_tokens(imgs_tr[sidx_tr[idx]])
    k = int(torch.randint(2, 37, (1,)))
    keep = torch.rand(batch_size, 36, device=device).topk(k, dim=1).indices.sort(dim=1).values
    vis = torch.gather(vis_all, 1, keep[:, :, None].expand(-1, -1, vis_all.size(2)))
    logits = model(text[:, :-1], vis, keep)
    loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, logits.size(-1)), text[:, 1:].reshape(-1), reduction="none")
    loss = (loss * mask[:, 1:].reshape(-1)).sum() / mask[:, 1:].sum()
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0); opt.step()
    if step in (1, 500, 1000, 1500):
        print(f"fine-tuning step {step:4d} | loss {loss.item():.4f}")

for name, color in (("random", "#d95f02"), ("content-based", "#08519c")):
    before = [100 * mean4(r) for r in before_ft[name]]
    after = [100 * mean4(r) for r in prune_results[name]]
    ax.plot(ks, before, "o--", color=color, lw=1.5, alpha=0.7, label=f"{name}, original model")
    ax.plot(ks, after, "o-", color=color, lw=2, label=f"{name}, after token-dropout fine-tuning")
ax.invert_xaxis(); ax.set_xlabel("visual tokens kept (of 36)"); ax.set_ylabel("mean accuracy (%)")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="lower left")

The change is large. With 12 of 36 tokens, accuracy goes from about 67% to about 92%, and with 24 tokens it is 98%. Once the model has been given a chance to adapt, keeping 24 of the 36 tokens costs under two points of accuracy, and keeping only 12 costs about eight. At the extreme, with only 2 tokens, random selection still reaches 74% of questions, since a pair of tokens that have attended to the whole image carry a good deal of information, and two random patches often capture something.

The fine-tuned model also contains a result that is easy to miss and informative. After fine-tuning, random selection beats content-based selection at small budgets: 79.6% against 66.1% with 4 tokens, and 73.8% against 58.1% with 2. Before fine-tuning, the content rule had been better. The likely reason has two parts. The model was fine-tuned on random subsets, so a content-selected subset is unfamiliar to it, which is a mismatch between how the model was prepared and how tokens are chosen at test time. And ranking patches by how much ink they contain is not a good way to cover a scene: squares have far more ink per patch than circles or triangles, so a small budget can be spent entirely on one or two shapes, leaving the model blind to the others. I did not run an experiment to separate these two effects, so treat this as a likely explanation and not as a result. The practical lesson is the same either way. A pruning rule should match how the model was trained, and a rule based only on importance can lose to a random one when it ignores coverage.

The contrastive alternative

Before the summary, here is the other family in code. CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder so that, among a batch of \(N\) image-text pairs, each image is most similar to its own caption and each caption to its own image. If \(u_i\) and \(v_j\) are the normalized image and text embeddings, the loss for the image side is a cross-entropy over the batch:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{image}} = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log \frac{\exp(u_i \cdot v_i / \tau)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} \exp(u_i \cdot v_j / \tau)},\]

where \(\tau\) is a temperature. The text side is the same with the roles swapped, and the two are averaged [1]. Each example is a classification problem in which the other \(N - 1\) items in the batch serve as negatives. In code, it is short:

import math, torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def clip_loss(img_emb, txt_emb, temperature=0.07):
    """Symmetric contrastive loss: matching image-text pairs are the 'correct class' in a batch of N pairs."""
    img = F.normalize(img_emb, dim=-1)
    txt = F.normalize(txt_emb, dim=-1)
    logits = img @ txt.T / temperature              # (N, N): entry (i, j) is the similarity of image i and text j
    labels = torch.arange(len(img))                 # the right partner of image i is text i
    return (F.cross_entropy(logits, labels) + F.cross_entropy(logits.T, labels)) / 2

torch.manual_seed(0)
N, d = 64, 128
a, b = torch.randn(N, d), torch.randn(N, d)
print(f"unrelated embeddings, temperature 1: loss {clip_loss(a, b, 1.0):.3f}  (chance level ln N = {math.log(N):.3f})")
print(f"identical embeddings, temperature 0.07: loss {clip_loss(a, a):.4f}")
print(f"identical embeddings, temperature 1: loss {clip_loss(a, a, 1.0):.3f}")

unrelated embeddings, temperature 1: loss 4.162  (chance level ln N = 4.159)
identical embeddings, temperature 0.07: loss 0.0001
identical embeddings, temperature 1: loss 3.190

The checks show what to expect. With unrelated embeddings the model is guessing among 64 partners and the loss is \(\ln 64 \approx 4.16\). With perfectly matched embeddings and a low temperature the loss is essentially zero. And the temperature matters: with \(\tau = 1\) even perfect matches give a high loss, because the softmax over cosine similarities, which lie in \([-1, 1]\), cannot become sharp. CLIP learns \(\tau\) as a parameter instead of fixing it [1]. A later variant, SigLIP, replaces the softmax over the batch with an independent sigmoid loss on each pair [10].

What real VLMs add

Our model has the full structure of a prefix-style VLM, and the real ones differ mostly in scale and in how they are trained.

  • Pretrained parts. The image encoder is typically a large vision transformer pretrained with a contrastive objective, and the language model is a pretrained LLM. Only the connection between them, and sometimes a fine-tuning stage over the whole system, is trained on the vision-language data.
  • Two-stage training. A common recipe first trains only the projector on image-caption pairs, so that visual features land in a region of the embedding space the language model can use, and then trains the projector and the language model on instruction-following data about images [2] [6].
  • Resolution and layout. Real images are larger, come in different shapes, and often contain text. Many systems cut them into tiles, each processed as its own set of tokens, which makes the token budget discussed above a first-order concern.
  • Known weaknesses. VLMs still describe objects that are not there, miscount, and struggle with fine spatial relationships. Our toy world is built to avoid exactly those difficulties, which is why it is not a measure of real capability.

Common implementation errors

  • Computing the loss on the question as well as the answer. The model then spends capacity learning to predict prompts, and the reported loss is hard to interpret. Mask the prompt.
  • Misaligned shifts. The logits at position \(t\) predict the token at \(t+1\). With a visual prefix of length \(k\), the slice of the output that corresponds to text starts at index \(k\), and an off-by-one here still trains but quietly learns the wrong thing.
  • Changing image normalization between training and evaluation. Pixel scaling is part of the model. If the evaluation images are scaled differently, accuracy drops for reasons that have nothing to do with learning.
  • Losing positions after pruning. If tokens are dropped and the survivors are renumbered, the position information changes. We keep each token’s original index.
  • Evaluating only with the image present. Always run the control with a mismatched or blank image. A model that has learned to answer from text priors can look good on a benchmark where questions leak the answers.
  • Testing on the training scenes. Keep a held-out set of images, and if you can, hold out combinations of attributes as well.

Exercises

  1. Compositional generalization. Remove all training images that contain a yellow circle, then ask the trained model about yellow circles in the test set. Does the model compose its notion of “yellow” and “circle”?
  2. Frozen parts. Freeze the language model and train only the projector and encoder, or the reverse. How much of the work does each part do?
  3. Fewer patches. Use \(16 \times 16\) patches, giving 9 tokens, and find where accuracy begins to fall.
  4. Contrastive pretraining. Train the vision encoder first with the contrastive loss on the captions, then use it in the generative model. Does it train faster?

References

  2. H. Liu, C. Li, Q. Wu, and Y. J. Lee. “Visual Instruction Tuning.” NeurIPS, 2023. arXiv:2304.08485
  3. J.-B. Alayrac et al. “Flamingo: a Visual Language Model for Few-Shot Learning.” NeurIPS, 2022. arXiv:2204.14198
  4. J. Li, D. Li, S. Savarese, and S. Hoi. “BLIP-2: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training with Frozen Image Encoders and Large Language Models.” ICML, 2023. arXiv:2301.12597
  5. A. Dosovitskiy et al. “An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale.” ICLR, 2021. arXiv:2010.11929
  6. H. Liu, C. Li, Y. Li, and Y. J. Lee. “Improved Baselines with Visual Instruction Tuning.” CVPR, 2024. arXiv:2310.03744
  7. L. Chen et al. “An Image is Worth 1/2 Tokens After Layer 2: Plug-and-Play Inference Acceleration for Large Vision-Language Models.” ECCV, 2024. arXiv:2403.06764
  8. D. Bolya, C.-Y. Fu, X. Dai, P. Zhang, C. Feichtenhofer, and J. Hoffman. “Token Merging: Your ViT But Faster.” ICLR, 2023. arXiv:2210.09461
  9. T. Darcet, M. Oquab, J. Mairal, and P. Bojanowski. “Vision Transformers Need Registers.” ICLR, 2024. arXiv:2309.16588
